key_facts: Former minister Alan Milburn's review of young people not in employment, education or training (NEET) recommends that large employers give all unsuccessful job applicants under 25 "meaningful feedback", with the aim of reducing the NEET share from 13% to about 5% by 2036; the proposals mainly concern England, with Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland asked to adapt them.

key_facts: A BBC test asked four AI models (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Alexa) to find a 55-inch TV deal a week before Black Friday, using free versions of the tools; the test was not a rigorous scientific study.

A recent YouGov survey of 19 countries ranked the UK second-last in the share of people who said they used AI to help them shop; 36% of respondents planning Black Friday shopping did not intend to use an AI tool.

Results were inconsistent: several recommended products were no longer listed, sold out, or priced differently from what the chatbots stated (e.g. a Currys price was £60 higher than the chatbot claimed), while Alexa's prices were correct but it only searched Amazon's own store.
Tech journalist Alex Hughes said AI saved him time in finding a TV via ChatGPT's agentic mode, but said that with live price data the results 'will be inconsistent and quite often incorrect'.
importance_reason: Consumer-tech feature article about AI shopping tools; no direct market-moving effect.

key_facts: Italian jeweller Paolo Bulgari, Chairman of the Bvlgari Group since 1984, died in Rome aged 89; the family announced the news.
The company was founded in Rome in the late 19th century by his grandfather, Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris, who later adapted the name to Bulgari in Italian.
In 2011 the family sold its controlling stake to the French luxury group LVMH in a deal worth about 3.7 billion euros; in 2019 Paolo Bulgari and his wife established the Paolo Bulgari Foundation.
The funeral is scheduled for Monday, 23 November in the Basilica of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, Rome.
importance_reason: Obituary of a company founder/chairman; no market-moving event, though it references the 2011 LVMH stake sale.

key_facts: Guernsey and Jersey published plans to allow approved applicants (journalists, academics, others with a legitimate interest) access to beneficial ownership information on companies when investigating suspected financial crime.

Sir Andrew Mitchell said the proposals 'do not go nearly far enough', warned limits on access could mean 'national security threats may remain entirely invisible to investigators', and called for information to be 'free at the point of access' and eventually fully public registers.

Jersey's consultation response requires applicants to show that 'all reasonable alternative sources have been exhausted'; Guernsey's published response does not explicitly set out the same requirement, per the BBC.

Both governments rejected the criticism, stating they continue to meet international standards on transparency and countering money laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing; Guernsey cited a positive 2025 assessment and said the proposal is based on a 'tried and tested model adopted in the EU'.
importance_reason: Регуляторная новость о прозрачности бенефициарного владения в Crown Dependencies с ограниченным прямым рыночным эффектом; политическая критика без признаков системного влияния.

key_facts: Centrica boss Chris O'Shea said he is "hugely concerned" about the expected substantial increase in energy bills from January, which he said was "materially correct" per predictions; the first quarter is when most energy is consumed.

Consultancy Cornwall Insight forecasts Ofgem's energy price cap will rise by 26% to £2,166 a year for a typical household from 1 January, an increase of £443 a year; the new cap is to be announced on Wednesday.
The amount owed to energy suppliers by households hit £5bn in the April to June period, according to Ofgem. Wholesale energy prices have risen this year due to the conflict in the Middle East.

The government will provide a £100 payment to some households and temporarily cut VAT on electricity from 5%, expected to save a typical household about £45 a year until the end of June next year; Citizens Advice called the £100 a "drop in the ocean".
